“Am I home?”

Marcus’s voice came out as a scratchy whisper, still rough from the chemicals used in reanimation. He sounded a hundred years old instead of twenty-seven.

That isn’t my voice, is it?

He blinked through fresh tears as sunlight seared eyes that had not seen it for a millennium. Gradually, the green and brown shapes sharpened into autumn leaves. Branches swayed above him, their rustling like dry parchment.

Earth. The familiarity eased his fear, but his joints ached as he tried to move.

He turned toward the silver, teardrop-shaped craft. Half buried at the end of the ravine it had gouged into the earth, it offered no answer to the question taking shape in his mind.

How long have I been away?

He tested his strength and winced. His one-piece Gore-Tex outfit pulled tight as he moved, adding irritation to the pain.

A familiar voice returned from a distant briefing: after cryogenic sleep, his body would need time to adjust. He would not have aged, but waking would have its unpleasant side effects.

Here I am, he thought, managing a smile as he studied the forest.

Furnace light filled the workshop. Marcus stood over the craftsman’s table, listening to the rhythm of the smiths’ hammers as they worked metal, crystal resin, and carbon into long, slender blades. Recipes unused since the Mage Wars were taking shape again, following designs he had drawn from memories that were not his own.

Nearby, leatherworkers stitched silver and crystal into the armor. Beneath Marcus’s skin, blue runes pulsed with the flow of power. The workers told stories of ancient runic mages who could fly and throw buildings. He smiled at the tales, unsure how much to believe.

His own experiments had already exceeded anything he had imagined. Now he understood how the Seer, using an imperfect version of the same process, had so easily overpowered him. The Silvans had made Marcus feel damn near invincible.

“Master Mage, your blades are complete.”

He turned toward the tall, stout master smith. Her white hair was tied back in a tight ponytail. Durass had sent two of his finest smiths, and their work had justified his confidence.

She placed the blades in Marcus’s outstretched hands. He admired them for a moment, then carried them to the table where the other components lay.

“Master Mage, I noticed the unusual layering of runes,” she said. “May I ask what they do?”

“It’s a technique few have used,” Marcus replied. “The spells for defense and offense are interwoven so that they feed off one another. The first people used it.”

He left the rest unsaid. Inscribing the pattern required more than knowing its shape. He could see power flowing through the runes, a gift that let him understand their relationships as he worked.

A scream came from above. Nero looked up. One of the creatures crouched on the broken roof.

It leaped before he could move, landing directly in front of him. Corpse-white skin stretched over its long limbs. It hissed and reached for him.

The anger he had carried for months broke loose.

Nero threw himself at the creature, catching it around the neck. They fell together. He slid his hands over its face.

“No more,” he whispered. “No more.”

His thumbs found its eyes. He pushed until the soft resistance gave way and warm black blood spilled over his hands. The creature bucked beneath him. Its claws tore through his robes and into his skin, but he scarcely felt them.

He gripped its head, raised it, and slammed it against the floor. Again. Again. The creature mewled and thrashed until a crack sounded beneath his hands.

Then it lay still.

Nero smiled. They could be hurt. They could be killed.

He lifted his blood-blackened hands toward the moon and screamed.

Above him, eight creatures crouched along the broken roof. As his cries echoed through the hall, they slipped away into the night.
